extracted.intended_audience: improvisational actors, theatre teachers, comedians, and improv students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for performing and teaching theatrical improvisation, emphasizing status mechanics, spontaneity, acceptance, physicality, and exercises to unblock imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status transactions as primary engine
rubrics_metrics.description: Many behaviors are driven by the desire to achieve a particular level of status; people continually raise and lower status in conversation and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every movement and inflection implies a status; perceiving scenes through status transactions changes how you direct, act, and write. Evaluate scenes by how clearly and inventively they display status flows and adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance / Say yes (yielding) vs blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Say yes to more and stop blocking the opportunities that come your way; yielding allows action to develop on stage that would be suppressed in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-status players tend to block; low-status players tend to accept. A good improvisor accepts offers to build scenes. Blocking is an anti-pattern that kills spontaneity; assess performers on their frequency of acceptance and ability to build on partners' offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of status (play high/low deliberately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Status is something one does: you may be low in social position but play high, and vice versa; moment-by-moment people adjust status fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should control status through actions, posture, and tone. Exercises (e.g., deliberately inserting hesitations or keeping head still) reveal perceived status shifts. Evaluate clarity and intentionality of status playing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status reversal as source of comedy and drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often arises when someone loses status; tragedy works on the same see-saw principle—ousting a high-status animal produces powerful emotional responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good play ingeniously displays and reverses status between characters; judges/teachers should look for inventive reversals and the audience's sympathy/relief at status shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical signals and posture to convey status
rubrics_metrics.description: Body posture (fear-crouch vs cherub posture), eye contact, and physical openness imply status; dark glasses raise status because they hide submission in the eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess performers on physical clarity: whether posture, eye contact, and movement consistently signal intended status. Examples: fear-crouch protects; cherub posture exposes and signals vulnerability/tenderness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enactment over discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: What happened matters, not what anybody said about it; banish aimless discussion and turn meetings/rehearsals into enactment sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer exercises and scenes that produce action rather than talk about action. Evaluate groups on whether they solve problems by doing rather than debating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupting routines to generate narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A routine interrupted creates a story; as a story progresses it establishes new routines which must then be broken to sustain interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for scenes that introduce clear routines and then puncture them; simple, obvious interruptions often produce immediate narrative. Examples: everyday routine disrupted by unexpected role or event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be obvious — accept first thoughts; don't over-intellectualize
rubrics_metrics.description: The more obvious an improviser is, the more original he appears; inspiration isn't intellectual — accept first thoughts rather than searching for cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: performers who censor their first impulses to appear original. Reward performers who act on first ideas and appear authentic. Evaluate degree of self-censorship versus spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relearn perception; fight education-induced dullness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dullness comes from education training us to see how things ought to be; improvisation teaching aims to relearn attending to the world as it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises should train attention to peripheral details and immediate perception (e.g., peripheral-vision exercise). Evaluate whether training restores fresh noticing and reduces formulaic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine imaginations additively (partner-triggering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining the imagination of two people should be additive rather than subtractive; if stuck, trigger your partner's ability to give 'unthought' answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate collaboration: do partners build on each other's offers to expand a scene rather than negate or control? Look for techniques that elicit partner creativity instead of suppressing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher's role: lower own displayed status to reduce fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher can sit on the floor and play low status physically while accepting blame for failures so students relax and risk failing without shame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess teaching approach by how well it dissolves normal teacher-student hierarchy and reduces performance anxiety. Anti-pattern: authoritative teaching that increases fear of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive, direct feedback in training
rubrics_metrics.description: Train to make positive comments and be direct (e.g., say 'Good' instead of 'That's enough').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate feedback style: concise, encouraging, and clear corrections are preferred over negative or vague critiques that stifle play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow actors to discover rather than demonstrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors/teachers should avoid demonstrating moves; allow actors to make their own discoveries so they feel ownership of choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: pre-blocking every move in rehearsal. Reward facilitation that lets performers find solutions; this increases spontaneity and commitment onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination is not one's personality; reduce ownership/anxiety over content
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should realize (1) they struggle against imagination, (2) they are not responsible for the content of their imaginations, (3) imagination is their true self rather than their taught 'personality'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate psychological readiness: ability to relinquish ownership of ideas, tolerate surprising or embarrassing content, and accept internal images without self-judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content comes from structure and what happens, not words alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Content lies in the structure — in what happens — not in what the characters say; even simple signs carry content apart from assigned meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scenes for strong structural events and physical actions that create meaning beyond dialogue. Reward clarity of sequence and causal action over clever lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exaggerated status gaps for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerated status gaps (e.g., servants elevating masters, absurd ceremonial trappings) often produce comedy because of contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for heightened contrasts and their timing; examples drawn from historical anecdotes (servants holding spittoons, etc.). Evaluate how well performers exploit and then subvert these gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and perceptual exercises to unblock creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical exercises—fixing eyes on an object while attending to the periphery, making tentative 'er' sounds, deliberately keeping the head still—trick the mind out of habitual dulling and reveal status effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether exercises are used regularly to heighten perception and loosen habitual behaviors. Successful practice produces observable changes in acceptance, richness of offers, and physical presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain relaxation when exposing anxiety-provoking material
rubrics_metrics.description: Use progressive, relaxed exposure (Wolpe-style) so relaxation is incompatible with anxiety; present milder forms and maintain relaxation to dissipate alarm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or performing material that might trigger fear, judge leaders on their ability to keep performers relaxed and to scale exposure appropriately. Failure to maintain relaxation is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and avoiding hubris in performance progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups can improve performance over iterations until hubris sets in, causing loss of humility and decline in quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ensembles for humility, openness to feedback, and avoidance of complacency. Monitor for signs of entitlement that degrade collaboration and risk-taking.
